screens.title: Least Privilege — Definition and Application
screens.narratorSegment: Least privilege means intentionally limiting permissions so users, roles, and services can do only what they must to perform their function. Practically, that means IAM policies scoped to actions and resources, security groups that only open necessary ports between explicitly identified peers, and resource policies that limit who can call which actions. A concrete example: instead of assigning s3:* to a role, restrict it to s3:GetObject on a single bucket path that your application reads. This limits the blast radius if credentials leak. Another example at the network level: allow web servers to talk to your app servers only on the application port, and deny all other inbound traffic to app and database tiers. A common misconception is thinking broad read permissions are harmless — they are not. Excessive read scope reveals data and metadata that attackers can use for lateral movement. To design least privilege, start by mapping required actions and flows for each component, then translate those into IAM and security group rules. Regularly review and test policies because requirements drift. Your takeaway: least privilege reduces what an attacker can do with a single compromised identity. Which role in your environment can you tighten today to reduce risk?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Least Privilege
Definition and rationale

Least privilege confines identities and services to the narrowest set of permissions required. This reduces exposure when credentials or services are compromised.

Concrete example
Grant an application role only s3:GetObject on a single bucket path instead of broad s3:* permissions across all buckets.
Common misconception
Permissive read permissions are low risk. In reality, data discovery and metadata access can assist attackers and enable lateral movement.
Key Takeaway
Start with deny-all, add allow rules after mapping exact needs, then continuously tighten.
Apply across layers
  • Identity: granular IAM policies and role separation.
  • Network: security groups referencing other SGs, not IP ranges when possible.
  • Resource: S3 bucket policies limiting actions and principals.
Design prompt
List one role and three actions it requires. For each action, specify the narrowest resource ARN or security group that satisfies the requirement.

screens.title: Creating Micro‑segmentation with Security Groups
screens.narratorSegment: Micro‑segmentation breaks networks into small zones and enforces explicit communication paths. In a typical three‑tier web application, you create three security groups: WebTierSG, AppTierSG, and DBTierSG. WebTierSG permits HTTP/HTTPS from the internet and outbound only to AppTierSG on the application port. AppTierSG allows inbound only from WebTierSG on the app port and outbound only to DBTierSG on the database port. DBTierSG only allows inbound from AppTierSG. A useful process is: first inventory the ports and protocols your components need; second, define the minimal security group relationships; third, apply rules referencing security group IDs rather than broad CIDR ranges; fourth, attach the groups and test connectivity. A common error is configuring broad outbound rules like allowing all traffic — that undermines segmentation. For example, if web servers are allowed to reach arbitrary IPs, a compromised web server could reach management endpoints. Verification: confirm that attempts to reach app or DB ports directly from the internet fail, while flows from web to app and app to DB succeed. This structure supports zero‑trust by default: every flow is explicit and auditable. What small change would reduce your blast radius further?

keyIdea.title: Explicit flows
keyIdea.text: Micro‑segmentation enforces explicit, auditable communication paths using security groups that reference each other rather than open networks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Micro-segmentation Process
Step-by-step
1. Inventory ports and flows
List exactly which ports each tier needs to accept and initiate.
2. Define security groups and rules
Create WebTierSG, AppTierSG, DBTierSG with inbound/outbound rules referencing each other.
3. Attach and verify
Attach SGs to instances and run connectivity checks and log reviews.
4. Harden and monitor
Remove unnecessary outbound rules and feed VPC Flow Logs into monitoring to detect anomalies.
Example rule set (conceptual)
WebTierSG inbound: HTTP/HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. WebTierSG outbound: Custom TCP port 8080 to AppTierSG. AppTierSG inbound: Custom TCP 8080 from WebTierSG. AppTierSG outbound: TCP 3306 to DBTierSG. DBTierSG inbound: TCP 3306 from AppTierSG.
Check your understanding
Why reference another security group as the source instead of using an IP range? Answer: SG references remain accurate as instances scale and they bind access to an identity boundary rather than mutable IPs.
Key Takeaway

Use SG references and restrict outbound traffic to prevent a compromised instance from reaching unexpected targets.

screens.title: Defense‑in‑Depth Layers
screens.narratorSegment: Defense‑in‑depth means layering protections so that if one control fails another mitigates the risk. Think of five core layers used in AWS architectures. The network layer uses VPCs, subnets, security groups, NACLs, WAF, Shield, and optionally a Transit Gateway to steer traffic. The compute layer relies on secure AMIs, IMDSv2 to protect instance metadata, host firewalls, vulnerability scanning, and anti‑malware controls. The data layer enforces encryption at rest with KMS or CloudHSM, encryption in transit with TLS, strict S3 bucket policies, and tools like Macie for sensitive data discovery. The identity layer enforces IAM roles, federation, MFA, and attribute‑based access control so every operation is authorized. Finally, logging and monitoring with CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Detective, and Security Hub provide detection and audit trails. A common misconception is believing one strong control replaces the rest; in practice, layered tools handle failures in different domains. For instance, if credentials are misused, network segmentation can limit movement while logging reveals actions for investigation. When you design, map each asset to which layers protect it and ensure logs flow to a centralized collector. Which layer would you add stronger telemetry to today?

keyIdea.text: Each layer protects different failure modes; together they reduce the chance of successful compromise and help with rapid detection and response.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Defense-in-Depth
Layer map
Network Layer
VPC, subnets, security groups, NACLs, WAF, Shield, Transit Gateway and inspection VPCs for central filtering.
Compute Layer
Hardened AMIs, IMDSv2, host firewalls, vulnerability scanning and endpoint protection.
Data Layer
KMS/CloudHSM encryption, TLS for transit, S3 policies, Object Lock, and data discovery tools.
Identity Layer
IAM roles, MFA, federation, ABAC and least privilege to control who can act on resources.
Logging & Monitoring
CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub, and centralized logging create detection, alerting and audit paths.
Practical tip
Map each asset to one or more layers and ensure logs for that layer are ingested into your central collector for correlation.
Common mistake
Relying on a single perimeter control and neglecting endpoint and data protections undermines defense-in-depth.

screens.title: Zero‑Trust Security Model
screens.narratorSegment: Zero‑trust rejects the notion that being inside a network boundary equals safety. Instead, every request is authenticated and authorized based on identity and context, regardless of origin. In AWS, this is implemented through strong identity controls like IAM roles, ABAC, MFA and short‑lived credentials, combined with micro‑segmentation to restrict what every workload can reach. Continuous monitoring is essential: GuardDuty, CloudTrail, and VPC Flow Logs provide the telemetry needed to validate that a request matches expected behavior. A concrete scenario: if a function attempts to access a database, the request should present a role with exact database permissions, the network path should be permitted only to that database, and the action should be logged and scanned for anomalies. A frequent misconception is to equate zero‑trust solely with network segmentation; it's actually identity‑first and requires both network and identity enforcement. To adopt zero‑trust incrementally, start by enforcing least privilege on service roles and adding SG references so only explicit peers communicate. How would you capture anomalies that indicate identity misuse in your environment? Zero‑Trust Security Model means zero‑trust treats identity as the primary control and uses continuous verification plus micro‑segmentation to limit risk.. In practical terms, never trust; always verify. identity and continuous validation at every request.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Zero‑Trust
What zero‑trust requires
  • Strong identity: roles, ABAC, short‑lived credentials, and MFA.
  • Micro‑segmentation: security groups and VPC boundaries that make flows explicit.
  • Continuous validation: telemetry and automated detection to verify behavior.
Concrete scenario
A Lambda function must assume a role limited to DynamoDB actions and call the table only via a VPC endpoint and an SG that permits that traffic. Logs and GuardDuty alerts validate the action.
Misconception
Zero‑trust is not only a network policy. Without identity controls and telemetry, segmentation alone is insufficient.
Practice prompt
Identify one high‑risk role and plan two steps to add continuous verification: stricter IAM conditions and additional logging for that role's operations.

screens.title: Secure Data Layer Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Protecting data requires controls both at rest and in motion, plus discovery and retention safeguards. For encryption at rest you should use KMS or CloudHSM to manage keys and apply server‑side encryption on S3, databases, and storage. Encryption in transit uses TLS to prevent eavesdropping between clients and services. Access policies should limit who can perform decrypt operations; for example, a compute role may have permission to use a KMS key for decryption but not key administration. Tools like Macie can discover sensitive objects and help apply Object Lock or lifecycle rules for compliance. A common error is encrypting data but leaving overly permissive S3 bucket policies — encryption plus least privilege is required. Also consider that encryption does not replace access controls; a key handed to a compromised role still allows data access. A practical design step is to map sensitive data locations, assign KMS keys with appropriate grant permissions, and ensure all in‑flight channels use TLS. How would you balance key separation and operational complexity for multiple datasets? Secure Data Layer Controls means combine encryption with strict access policies and discovery tools so encrypted data remains protected against misuse and leakage.. In practical terms, encrypt, discover, and protect sensitive data at rest and in transit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Data Layer Controls
Core practices
  • Encrypt at rest with KMS/CloudHSM and enforce least privilege on key usage.
  • Use TLS for all in‑flight traffic and validate certificates.
  • Use discovery tools to find sensitive objects and apply Object Lock where required.
Example checklist
Map buckets and databases, assign KMS keys per sensitivity level, restrict decrypt to specific roles, enable Macie scanning, and review S3 policies for public access.
Key Takeaway
Encryption is most effective when combined with least privilege and discovery controls to limit who can use keys and access objects.

screens.title: Compute Layer Protections and IMDSv2
screens.narratorSegment: The compute layer must be hardened to prevent an attacker from moving laterally or extracting secrets. Hardened AMIs reduce exposure by baking in security updates and configuration baselines. Use IMDSv2 on EC2 to require session authentication for instance metadata, mitigating server‑side request forgery that can leak credentials. Host‑based firewalls, anti‑malware, and continuous vulnerability scanning detect and contain threats on instances. A practical example: deploy a secure AMI, configure IMDSv2 so applications obtain credentials via temporary sessions, and run Inspector to flag missing patches or vulnerable packages. A misconception is believing instance hardening is a one‑time task; it's ongoing. Also, assume that a compromised instance can attempt outbound connections — limit outbound rules and use VPC egress controls to reduce the impact. Map which instances require EDR agents or stricter isolation. The design tradeoff is between ease of operations and risk reduction; automated patching and image pipelines help keep that balance. What detection signal would you add to identify an unusual process on a compute node? Compute Layer Protections and IMDSv2 means use secure images, imdsv2, host protections, and scanning to reduce the chance and impact of compute compromises.. In practical terms, harden instances, protect metadata, and run vulnerability scanning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Compute Protections
Key controls
  • Hardened AMIs and automated image pipelines.
  • IMDSv2 enforced so metadata requires session tokens.
  • Host firewalls, EDR/antivirus, and vulnerability scanning (Inspector).
Operational prompts
Add IMDSv2 enforcement to instance launch templates, document which roles need instance profile access, and limit outbound egress for critical instances.

screens.title: Security Reference Architectures — Web, Data Lake, Serverless
screens.narratorSegment: Security reference architectures offer repeatable blueprints that map AWS services to control points. For a secure web application, combine CloudFront with WAF and Shield for edge protection, use ALB to terminate TLS, place EC2 or ECS tasks in private subnets behind the ALB, and run the database in a private subnet with KMS encryption. Apply least privilege on task roles and centralize logs to CloudWatch and CloudTrail. For a data lake, use encrypted S3 buckets with Lake Formation controlling table-level access, Glue for ETL with restricted roles, and Athena or Redshift Spectrum for queries with KMS keys and auditing enabled. For serverless apps, use A P I Gateway with WAF, Cognito for authentication, Lambda with least-privilege roles, DynamoDB with server‑side encryption and fine-grained IAM controls, and ensure all function activity is logged. The pattern across these blueprints is to combine network isolation, strict identity, encryption, and centralized logging. A common oversight is leaving management endpoints reachable from less-secure networks; ensure bastion hosts or session managers are used for administrative access. screens.title: Inspection VPC and Transit Gateway Integration
screens.narratorSegment: An inspection VPC hosts third‑party firewalls and inspection appliances to centralize traffic filtering for multiple VPCs. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore the principles and patterns that turn individual security controls into a resilient architecture. We begin with two foundational ideas: least privilege, which reduces exposure by granting only necessary permissions, and defense-in-depth, which layers protections so a single failure does not lead to compromise. You will also learn how zero‑trust reframes decisions by treating every request as untrusted until proven otherwise, and how micro‑segmentation enforces that model at the network layer. Practical reference architectures follow: secure web applications, data lakes, and serverless applications with concrete control points like KMS for encryption and IAM roles for identity. Finally, we'll cover how to integrate third‑party Marketplace solutions into an inspection VPC connected through Transit Gateway without creating blind spots. Throughout, notice common mistakes such as overly permissive policies or relying solely on network boundaries. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to design multi‑tier security controls, map them to AWS services, and verify that your architecture reduces blast radius and supports continuous monitoring. Consider which area in your current architecture would most benefit from immediate micro‑segmentation.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply least privilege and defense‑in‑depth to multi‑tier architectures, implement zero‑trust using micro‑segmentation and identity controls, design secure reference architectures for web, data lake, and serverless use cases, and evaluate Marketplace security solutions for integration into a centralized inspection model. Each objective maps to concrete skills: crafting granular IAM policies that limit actions and resources, composing layered controls across network, compute, data, identity, and logging, and building VPC segmentation where each tier communicates only with explicitly authorized peers. You will practice a hands‑on scenario: create three security groups that enforce the exact allowed paths between web, app, and database tiers and verify that direct internet access to internal tiers is blocked. You will also assess when to deploy an inspection VPC with Transit Gateway to centralize third‑party firewall inspection and how to ensure those tools feed into your logging and detection pipeline. Finally, you will learn common pitfalls such as excessive permissions and single points of failure, and how to detect them with continuous monitoring. Which objective aligns with your immediate environment and why might that matter?

This page explains the practical outcomes you will practice. You will design security groups that strictly allow only the necessary flows between web, application, and database tiers and attach them to placeholder instances to validate connectivity. You will also map layered controls to AWS services: VPCs and security groups at the network layer, hardened AMIs and IMDSv2 for compute, KMS and object‑level policies for data, and GuardDuty and CloudTrail for monitoring. Verification is essential: simulated connectivity checks and audit trails confirm that rules behave as intended, while centralized logging surfaces configuration drift. The exercise includes common verification steps: attempt internet access to private tiers to confirm it is blocked, and check that only allowed security group IDs are accepted as sources or destinations. Finally, you'll practice evaluating a Marketplace firewall by ensuring it supports IAM‑based integration, scales behind Transit Gateway, and forwards logs to your central collector. These verification skills ensure your architecture not only looks secure on diagram, but enforces policy in production. Which verification step will you run first in your environment?

Least privilege means intentionally limiting permissions so users, roles, and services can do only what they must to perform their function. Practically, that means IAM policies scoped to actions and resources, security groups that only open necessary ports between explicitly identified peers, and resource policies that limit who can call which actions. A concrete example: instead of assigning s3:* to a role, restrict it to s3:GetObject on a single bucket path that your application reads. This limits the blast radius if credentials leak. Another example at the network level: allow web servers to talk to your app servers only on the application port, and deny all other inbound traffic to app and database tiers. A common misconception is thinking broad read permissions are harmless — they are not. Excessive read scope reveals data and metadata that attackers can use for lateral movement. To design least privilege, start by mapping required actions and flows for each component, then translate those into IAM and security group rules. Regularly review and test policies because requirements drift. Your takeaway: least privilege reduces what an attacker can do with a single compromised identity. Which role in your environment can you tighten today to reduce risk?

Micro‑segmentation breaks networks into small zones and enforces explicit communication paths. In a typical three‑tier web application, you create three security groups: WebTierSG, AppTierSG, and DBTierSG. WebTierSG permits HTTP/HTTPS from the internet and outbound only to AppTierSG on the application port. AppTierSG allows inbound only from WebTierSG on the app port and outbound only to DBTierSG on the database port. DBTierSG only allows inbound from AppTierSG. A useful process is: first inventory the ports and protocols your components need; second, define the minimal security group relationships; third, apply rules referencing security group IDs rather than broad CIDR ranges; fourth, attach the groups and test connectivity. A common error is configuring broad outbound rules like allowing all traffic — that undermines segmentation. For example, if web servers are allowed to reach arbitrary IPs, a compromised web server could reach management endpoints. Verification: confirm that attempts to reach app or DB ports directly from the internet fail, while flows from web to app and app to DB succeed. This structure supports zero‑trust by default: every flow is explicit and auditable. What small change would reduce your blast radius further?

Defense‑in‑depth means layering protections so that if one control fails another mitigates the risk. Think of five core layers used in AWS architectures. The network layer uses VPCs, subnets, security groups, NACLs, WAF, Shield, and optionally a Transit Gateway to steer traffic. The compute layer relies on secure AMIs, IMDSv2 to protect instance metadata, host firewalls, vulnerability scanning, and anti‑malware controls. The data layer enforces encryption at rest with KMS or CloudHSM, encryption in transit with TLS, strict S3 bucket policies, and tools like Macie for sensitive data discovery. The identity layer enforces IAM roles, federation, MFA, and attribute‑based access control so every operation is authorized. Finally, logging and monitoring with CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Detective, and Security Hub provide detection and audit trails. A common misconception is believing one strong control replaces the rest; in practice, layered tools handle failures in different domains. For instance, if credentials are misused, network segmentation can limit movement while logging reveals actions for investigation. When you design, map each asset to which layers protect it and ensure logs flow to a centralized collector. Which layer would you add stronger telemetry to today?

Zero‑trust rejects the notion that being inside a network boundary equals safety. Instead, every request is authenticated and authorized based on identity and context, regardless of origin. In AWS, this is implemented through strong identity controls like IAM roles, ABAC, MFA and short‑lived credentials, combined with micro‑segmentation to restrict what every workload can reach. Continuous monitoring is essential: GuardDuty, CloudTrail, and VPC Flow Logs provide the telemetry needed to validate that a request matches expected behavior. A concrete scenario: if a function attempts to access a database, the request should present a role with exact database permissions, the network path should be permitted only to that database, and the action should be logged and scanned for anomalies. A frequent misconception is to equate zero‑trust solely with network segmentation; it's actually identity‑first and requires both network and identity enforcement. To adopt zero‑trust incrementally, start by enforcing least privilege on service roles and adding SG references so only explicit peers communicate. How would you capture anomalies that indicate identity misuse in your environment? Zero‑Trust Security Model means zero‑trust treats identity as the primary control and uses continuous verification plus micro‑segmentation to limit risk.. In practical terms, never trust; always verify. identity and continuous validation at every request.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Protecting data requires controls both at rest and in motion, plus discovery and retention safeguards. For encryption at rest you should use KMS or CloudHSM to manage keys and apply server‑side encryption on S3, databases, and storage. Encryption in transit uses TLS to prevent eavesdropping between clients and services. Access policies should limit who can perform decrypt operations; for example, a compute role may have permission to use a KMS key for decryption but not key administration. Tools like Macie can discover sensitive objects and help apply Object Lock or lifecycle rules for compliance. A common error is encrypting data but leaving overly permissive S3 bucket policies — encryption plus least privilege is required. Also consider that encryption does not replace access controls; a key handed to a compromised role still allows data access. A practical design step is to map sensitive data locations, assign KMS keys with appropriate grant permissions, and ensure all in‑flight channels use TLS. How would you balance key separation and operational complexity for multiple datasets? Secure Data Layer Controls means combine encryption with strict access policies and discovery tools so encrypted data remains protected against misuse and leakage.. In practical terms, encrypt, discover, and protect sensitive data at rest and in transit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The compute layer must be hardened to prevent an attacker from moving laterally or extracting secrets. Hardened AMIs reduce exposure by baking in security updates and configuration baselines. Use IMDSv2 on EC2 to require session authentication for instance metadata, mitigating server‑side request forgery that can leak credentials. Host‑based firewalls, anti‑malware, and continuous vulnerability scanning detect and contain threats on instances. A practical example: deploy a secure AMI, configure IMDSv2 so applications obtain credentials via temporary sessions, and run Inspector to flag missing patches or vulnerable packages. A misconception is believing instance hardening is a one‑time task; it's ongoing. Also, assume that a compromised instance can attempt outbound connections — limit outbound rules and use VPC egress controls to reduce the impact. Map which instances require EDR agents or stricter isolation. The design tradeoff is between ease of operations and risk reduction; automated patching and image pipelines help keep that balance. What detection signal would you add to identify an unusual process on a compute node? Compute Layer Protections and IMDSv2 means use secure images, imdsv2, host protections, and scanning to reduce the chance and impact of compute compromises.. In practical terms, harden instances, protect metadata, and run vulnerability scanning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security reference architectures offer repeatable blueprints that map AWS services to control points. For a secure web application, combine CloudFront with WAF and Shield for edge protection, use ALB to terminate TLS, place EC2 or ECS tasks in private subnets behind the ALB, and run the database in a private subnet with KMS encryption. Apply least privilege on task roles and centralize logs to CloudWatch and CloudTrail. For a data lake, use encrypted S3 buckets with Lake Formation controlling table-level access, Glue for ETL with restricted roles, and Athena or Redshift Spectrum for queries with KMS keys and auditing enabled. These are the core ideas to keep in mind. First, least privilege shrinks an attacker’s options by granting only required permissions across IAM, network, and resources. Second, defense‑in‑depth layers different controls — network, compute, data, identity, and monitoring — so that a single failure is insufficient for compromise. Third, zero‑trust shifts the model to verify every request using strong identity controls and micro‑segmentation. Fourth, micro‑segmentation implemented with security groups and VPC boundaries limits lateral movement, enforcing explicit flows between tiers. Fifth, security reference architectures provide repeatable blueprints for secure web, data lake, and serverless deployments.
